title: A Harvest for the Winter
premise: Pest controller Marguerite Blackwood is called back to their late grandmother's farmhouse, where every family photograph has gained an empty chair that shouldn't exist — a chair that appears, closer each day, in the pictures of the living. Digging through grandma's ledgers, Marguerite discovers the family survived the Depression by 'inviting in' something that grants harvests in exchange for a seat at the table, and the debt has come due on the tenth anniversary of grandma's death. As the chair draws nearer and relatives begin to vanish into the photographs, Marguerite must choose between honoring the loyalty that kept the family fed and exposing the truth — ending with Marguerite offering their own chair, then refusing at the last moment, binding the thing to the house forever and walking out at sunrise with the photographs finally, terribly, empty.
about_author: Noor Whitlock is the pen name of a former insurance investigator who spent years cataloguing other people's disasters before turning them into fiction. They write horror rooted in rural decay, family debt, and the quiet violence of inheritance, and live somewhere with very old trees.

chapters.title: The Call You Don't Take Twice
chapters.summary: Marguerite, a pest controller with a reputation for handling 'unusual' jobs, receives a call about scratching in the walls of their late grandmother's farmhouse — a house that was supposedly sealed. POV Marguerite. The beat is dread disguised as routine; they take the job because refusing it feels impossible.

chapters.title: Fingerprints in the Dust
chapters.summary: At the farmhouse, Marguerite finds droppings that aren't droppings, gnaw marks at table height, and a fine dust on every chair — as if something sat down recently. POV Marguerite. The emotional beat is professional denial cracking: ten years of rational explanations begin to fail in a single afternoon.

chapters.title: The Extra Chair
chapters.summary: Reviewing old family photos for the estate lawyer, Marguerite notices an empty wooden chair in every image — including pictures taken decades apart, in different rooms, before the chair existed. POV Marguerite. The beat is vertigo: the past itself has been edited, and only Marguerite seems able to see it.

chapters.title: What Grandma Kept in the Cellar
chapters.summary: Marguerite searches the cellar and finds grandma's harvest ledgers: decades of impossible yields recorded beside a column marked only 'SEAT.' The final entry, ten years old, reads 'PAID IN FULL — ONE SEAT VACANT.' POV Marguerite. The beat is cold clarity — this was never a haunting; it's a contract.

chapters.title: Family Arrives for the Reading
chapters.summary: Relatives gather for the will: Uncle Dale, cousins Priya and Tom, and Aunt Rosalind, who refuses to enter the house and won't say why. POV Marguerite. The beat is tension under civility — everyone is performing normalcy, and everyone is watching the chairs.

chapters.title: The Will That Names a Piece of Furniture
chapters.summary: The lawyer reads the will: the farmhouse and 'its guest of honor' pass to Marguerite. Rosalind storms out; Dale laughs it off; Priya quietly asks Marguerite what grandma meant. POV Marguerite. The beat is inheritance as trap — the family has passed the debt down like an heirloom.

chapters.title: Rosalind's Warning
chapters.summary: Marguerite visits Rosalind, who was disinherited thirty years ago. She reveals she saw the chair move as a child and was called a liar; grandma chose her favorite as the new keeper instead. POV Rosalind. The beat is bitter vindication — the truth-teller punished, the loyal one rewarded.

chapters.title: First Night: The Sound of Being Seated
chapters.summary: Marguerite stays the night to 'finish the job.' At 3 a.m., the kitchen chair scrapes across the floor — toward the table — and stops. In the morning, a new photo on the mantel shows Marguerite asleep, and the chair is one step closer. POV Marguerite. The beat is violation: it has begun keeping its own album.

chapters.title: Priya's Photographs
chapters.summary: Priya, a photography student, digitizes the family archive and confirms the chair appears in photos spanning a century — always closer to the living subjects in the most recent ones. POV Priya. The beat is scholarly terror turning to resolve; she wants to document it, which may be exactly the wrong instinct.

chapters.title: Dale Makes a Deal
chapters.summary: Dale, drowning in debt, secretly offers himself to the house — he'll take the seat if the harvest continues. The house responds by making him the only relative the chair doesn't approach. POV Dale. The beat is corrosive self-interest; loyalty was always just leverage he hadn't cashed yet.

chapters.title: The Harvest That Shouldn't Have Grown
chapters.summary: The dead garden behind the house erupts in ripe vegetables overnight — the first 'payment' in ten years. The relatives gorge, then notice none of them can leave the property; the road loops back. POV Marguerite. The beat is gilded horror: the house feeds you while it closes its hands.

chapters.title: What Was Invited In
chapters.summary: In the ledgers' earliest pages, Marguerite finds 1931: grandma's father, starving, performed an invitation at the table and something answered — something that was hungry first, and polite second. POV Marguerite. The beat is inherited guilt; the family's survival was someone else's consumption, deferred.

chapters.title: Tom Disappears Into the Picture
chapters.summary: Cousin Tom mocks the whole affair, poses for a photo by the mantel, and is simply absent afterward — present in the image, seated in the chair, mouth open in a soundless scream. POV Priya. The beat is grief and guilt; her documentation gave it a doorway.

chapters.title: The House Rewrites Itself
chapters.summary: The farmhouse's interior begins shifting — rooms rearranging around the kitchen, walls hung with photos of every Blackwood who ever sat at that table, all watching. POV Marguerite. The beat is claustrophobic escalation; the house is not haunted by the thing, it is the thing.

chapters.title: Dale Takes the Chair
chapters.summary: Dale, believing he's secured a bargain, sits in the chair at midnight. The harvest blooms — and Dale is pulled into the newest photograph, his deal honored in the only currency the house accepts. POV Dale. The beat is tragic irony; he got exactly what he asked for and nothing he wanted.

chapters.title: Rosalind Returns
chapters.summary: Rosalind breaks her thirty-year exile and enters the house, armed with the only weapon she has: the truth, spoken aloud, that the family fed people to their own prosperity. The house recoils from her words. POV Rosalind. The beat is courage through bitterness — truth hurts the thing that runs on loyalty and silence.

chapters.title: The Seat at the Table
chapters.summary: The chair arrives at the head of the table, facing Marguerite's place. The remaining family must decide: offer someone, refuse together, or run. The road is gone; the walls are photographs now. POV Marguerite. The beat is the loyalty-versus-truth choice made flesh around a dinner table.

chapters.title: What Marguerite Offers
chapters.summary: Marguerite sits in the chair themselves, offering the seat as keeper — the house accepts, and begins to draw them into the album — while Priya and Rosalind speak the full truth of the ledgers aloud, name by name, victim by victim. POV Marguerite. The beat is sacrifice entwined with confession; the two weapons deployed at once.

chapters.title: The Refusal
chapters.summary: Half-photographed, Marguerite retracts the offer: the seat was accepted under false harvests built on stolen lives, and a contract fed by lies is void. The house screams in a century of recorded voices; the chair cracks down its spine. POV Marguerite. The beat is the climax — justice outside any law, spoken from inside the trap.

chapters.title: Sunrise on an Empty Table
chapters.summary: Dawn. The house is just a rotting farmhouse; every photograph is empty, the chair a pile of ash. Tom and Dale are gone — truly gone, unrecoverable. Marguerite, Priya, and Rosalind walk out through a garden gone to seed. POV Marguerite. The beat is hollow victory; truth freed them and cost what loyalty could not save.

chapters.title: The Estate, Settled
chapters.summary: Weeks later, Marguerite burns the ledgers, settles the estate, and gives Rosalind the deed she was cheated of. Priya's photos of the empty album are the only record. POV Priya. The beat is restitution — the inheritance finally passed honestly, to the one who was owed.

chapters.title: A Knock at the New Door
chapters.summary: In Marguerite's own apartment, a new photograph develops on Priya's forgotten film: Marguerite's kitchen, with a second chair. Marguerite sets it face-down and calls Rosalind — some truths must be kept spoken to stay true. POV Marguerite. The beat is a quiet, vigilant ending; the harvest is over, but winter is long.
